hints: Look at what is being made in this reaction, stable small molecules like $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ tell you a lot about heat change.
Recall that forming very stable products from less stable fragments and pollutants releases a lot of energy as heat.
Think about whether breaking bonds or forming stable products with negative $\Delta H_f^\ominus$ values drives the overall $\Delta H$ negative.
walkthrough:
**Decide if heat is released or absorbed**

Think like a combustion reaction. Unburnt fragments like $\text{CH}_3$ are being fully oxidised to $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Such complete oxidation to very stable products almost always releases heat, so $\Delta H$ is negative and exothermic.

**Use standard enthalpies of formation**

Recall the rule:
$$\Delta H_r^\ominus = \sum \Delta H_f^\ominus(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta H_f^\ominus(\text{reactants})$$
$\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ have large negative $\Delta H_f^\ominus$ values because they are very stable.

**Check the reasons for each row**

Breaking bonds always needs energy in, it cannot explain why a reaction gives energy out. Forming strong $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{O-H}$ bonds and a strong $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$ bond releases far more energy than is used to break $\text{NO}_2$.

So the reaction is exothermic because the products have negative formation enthalpies.

options.A: Incorrect energy change and incorrect reason. Converting chemical energy to heat energy describes an exothermic change where heat is given out, not an endothermic change where heat is taken in.
options.B: Incorrect energy change. A very high $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$ bond energy means a lot of energy is released when $\text{N}_2$ is formed, which favours an exothermic reaction, not an endothermic one.
options.C: Correct on both parts. The reaction makes $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ which have negative $\Delta H_f^\ominus$ values, so formation of these very stable products releases more energy than is needed to break bonds, giving an overall exothermic $\Delta H$.
options.D: Right label, wrong reason. Breaking double bonds in $\text{NO}_2$ requires energy input (endothermic step). It cannot be the reason the overall reaction is exothermic. The exothermicity comes from forming new strong bonds in $\text{CO}_2$, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{N}_2$.
